ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Hematology Referral — Robert Peary

code.originalText: Establishing primary care for four months of fatigue, breathlessness, pallor, a sore tongue, and numbness and unsteadiness in the feet: blood tests, neurological and foot examination, falls, mood, the first vitamin B12 injection and a hematology consultation

text.paragraph: Severe macrocytic anemia with low white cells and platelets, a vitamin B12 of 96 pg/mL and a high methylmalonic acid, with posterior column signs and numb, unsteady feet, in a 62-year-old retired naval officer with old frostbite amputations of the toes. Please confirm the cause and advise on treatment, endoscopy and follow-up. [S]
Urgency: Within one to two weeks; treatment started today. [S]

list.item: Is this pernicious anemia, and which tests confirm it?
What injection schedule and duration do you advise, and is oral therapy an option for him?
Does he need a transfusion, and what early complications of treatment should we watch for?
Does he need upper endoscopy, and what surveillance afterwards?
What other conditions should we screen for, and what recovery can he expect in his nerves and balance?

text.paragraph: Four months of fatigue, breathlessness on one flight of stairs, pallor with a lemon-yellow tinge, a sore tongue, about 2 kg of weight loss, and numbness, tingling and unsteadiness in the feet, worse in the dark; one fall a month ago without injury. No bleeding, black stools, fever or night sweats. No stomach surgery, metformin, acid-suppressing medicine or nitrous oxide; a mixed diet with meat and dairy; alcohol a few glasses of wine a week; never smoked. Toes two to five of each foot were amputated after frostbite in early middle age; a leg fracture above the ankle healed long ago. Examination: pale with slight scleral icterus, a smooth red tongue, pulse 102, blood pressure 124/66, a soft systolic flow murmur; vibration absent at the ankles, impaired joint position sense at the great toes, absent ankle jerks with brisk knee jerks, flexor plantars, positive Romberg; MoCA 27, PHQ-9 6. Results today: hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, MCV 118 fL, RDW 19.6%, white cells 3.4, platelets 118, reticulocytes 0.4%; smear with oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; LDH 1240 U/L, bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL; vitamin B12 96 pg/mL, methylmalonic acid 3.10 and homocysteine 38 µmol/L, folate 14.2 ng/mL; ferritin 62 ng/mL, saturation 55%; creatinine 0.98 mg/dL, potassium 4.1 mmol/L; TSH 2.6, HbA1c 5.5%. Started today after the blood was drawn: cyanocobalamin 1,000 micrograms into the muscle every other day for seven doses. No transfusion given [S]

list.item: Tired and breathless doing what used to be easy. [S]
Numb, unsteady feet on top of feet that lost their toes long ago. [S]
He wants to know whether this illness can be treated, and to keep walking and working. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Robert Edwin Peary was born on May 6, 1856, in Cresson, Pennsylvania. His father died within three years of his birth, and his mother raised him in southern Maine. [D]

He graduated from Bowdoin College as a civil engineer in 1877, joined the Coast and Geodetic Survey in Washington in 1879 and the U.S. Navy Civil Engineer Corps in 1881, and surveyed in Nicaragua for a proposed canal; there he hired Matthew Henson, the African American who proved indispensable to his Arctic work. [D]

From 1886 to 1909 he planned and led eight Arctic expeditions, one of them four years long, relying on the help of Inughuit (Polar Inuit) men and women of northwestern Greenland, who hunted, sledged, sewed and overwintered with his parties. On the 1891 to 1892 expedition he showed that Greenland is an island. [D]

On July 11, 1891, aboard the Kite in the ice of Melville Bay, the iron tiller, jammed over by an ice cake, caught his leg against the deckhouse and broke both bones just above the ankle; the leg was set and he was carried ashore at the winter camp. [D]

In 1897, at the request of staff of the American Museum of Natural History, who had asked for one Inughuit man to work with the museum for a year, he brought six Inughuit people from Greenland to New York: three men, a woman and two children. Within months four of them had died; a boy of about seven, whose father was among the dead, was left an orphan far from home, and the museum kept his father's bones instead of burying them. [D]

On the expedition of 1898 to 1902, reaching the old station at Fort Conger on Ellesmere Island at midnight on January 6, 1899, he found that both feet were frozen; in March a doctor amputated the affected toes. He lost most of his toes, and the stumps were often left bloody and aching by knocks against rough ice on later journeys. [D]
The number of toes he lost is uncertain: the roster says eight, and a historian of the expedition notes that the exact number and circumstances have been mythologized. [R]

He married in 1888 and had two children with his wife. He also had two sons with an Inughuit woman in Greenland, born during his expeditions; his daughter's papers name them as her half-brothers, and one of them was an infant in the winter of 1900 to 1901. [D]

On April 6, 1909, he reported reaching the North Pole with Matthew Henson and four Inughuit men, Ootah, Egingwah, Seegloo and Ooqueah (Odaq, Iggianguaq, Sigluk and Ukkujaaq in today's spelling). Frederick Cook announced a competing claim days before Peary returned; most geographic bodies came to credit Peary, but the claim has long been disputed. [D]

He retired from the Navy in 1911 as a rear admiral with the Thanks of Congress, and lived his last years with his family in Washington, D.C., spending summers on Eagle Island on the Maine coast; the dispute over his claim cast a pall over those years. [D]

Diagnosis: blood count with MCV, smear and reticulocytes; vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine and folate; iron studies, LDH and bilirubin; kidney function; TSH and HbA1c; all drawn before the first injection. Guideline: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders (2014); Vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s: diagnosis and management (NG239) (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Treatment started at intake without waiting for the cause, because of neurological signs: cyanocobalamin 1,000 micrograms into the muscle every other day for seven doses; no folic acid alone; no transfusion while he is stable at rest. Guideline: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders (2014); Vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s: diagnosis and management (NG239) (2024) [S]

Response and safety checks: reticulocytes and potassium in the first week, blood count at about five and eight weeks, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine and iron studies at eight weeks, and symptoms at every visit. Guideline: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders (2014); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Nerves and falls: neurological examination (vibration, joint position, reflexes, Romberg, gait, cognition) at each visit; physical therapy for balance and gait; night lights and a clear path at home; a stick outdoors and care on ice. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026); Falls Prevention in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Interventions (2024) [S]

Feet: daily skin checks with a mirror, extra-depth shoes with toe fillers and a forefoot rocker sole, no new boots without a fitting, nail and callus care by podiatry every three months, and same-day care for any blister, redness or wound. Guideline: Guidelines on the prevention of foot ulcers in persons with diabetes (IWGDF 2023 update) (2023) [S]

Mood and cognition: PHQ-9 and MoCA at intake and after treatment, since vitamin B12 deficiency can affect both. Guideline: Vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s: diagnosis and management (NG239) (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, anemia and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
